title: Domestic dogs descend from several wild species

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Domestic dogs descend from several wild species

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Domestic dogs have probably descended from several distinct wild species rather than from a single one.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: from geographical and other considerations, I think it highly probable that our domestic dogs have descended from several wild species.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter I, “Variation under Domestication”; section “Origin of Domestic Varieties from one or more Species”. Scope: domestic dogs and wild Canidae

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch01-09: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.90

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Extensive modern and ancient canid genomes are public, and standard admixture and demographic models directly distinguish the alternatives. Residual ambiguity concerns semantics of descent and extinct sources, not data availability.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Fit demographic ancestry models to whole genomes from global dogs and candidate wild canids, testing one-source against multiple-species ancestry. Significant ancestry from several distinct wild species supports the claim; a single ancestral species with later limited introgression refutes it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Ancient introgression can be confused with multiple domestication sources.

Extinct source populations may be unsampled.

fields.value:
operationalizability: 0.91
data existence: 0.95
data adequacy: 0.86
discriminating power: 0.9
analysis feasibility: 0.83

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Dog and wild canid genomes are public in the sequence archives, and ancestry graphs are a standard analysis a small team can rerun. The data cover major breed groups and the living wild species Darwin would have considered, with real gaps for extinct wolves. Those gaps and the species-versus-population ambiguity lower discriminating power without changing the fact that a single-species versus multi-species origin is directly testable now.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Estimate ancestry graphs for worldwide dog breeds against wild canids using public genomes. Descent from several wild species would be supported by substantial founding ancestry from two or more canid species; a single founding species, with only later minor admixture, would refute that reading.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Darwin's geographical 'species' may correspond to wolf populations that current taxonomy treats as one species.

Modern breed admixture with coyotes or jackals can be mistaken for a separate domestication origin.

Extinct Pleistocene wolf populations are unevenly sampled, so an unsampled source can look like a missing species.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
discriminating power: 0.78
data existence: 0.88
operationalizability: 0.9
data adequacy: 0.74
analysis feasibility: 0.8

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: If Darwin is right that domestic dogs descend from several distinct wild species (he had in mind wolves and jackals), then some domestic dog maternal lineages should trace to a wild canid species other than the grey wolf: a non-trivial fraction of dog mitochondrial genomes should be closer to Canis aureus, C. lupaster, C. latrans, C. simensis, Cuon alpinus or Lycaon pictus than to any wild Canis lupus.

fields.label: Method
fields.value: analysis.py runs eight esearch queries (complete mitochondrial genomes of dog, wild wolf, coyote, golden jackal, African wolf, Ethiopian wolf, dhole, African wild dog), takes every third dog UID (453 of 1,357) and all UIDs for the other groups, efetches GenBank flat files, extracts the CYTB and COX1 CDS from the feature table (IUPAC codes kept as N so coordinates are preserved), keeps records with the modal gene lengths (1,140 + 1,545 bp), and computes pairwise ungapped p-distances over the 2,685 bp concatenation. For each dog it records the distance to the nearest wild wolf and to the nearest sequence of each other species; the measured value is the number of dogs whose nearest non-dog sequence is not Canis lupus.

fields.label: Pass criterion
fields.value: Using complete mitochondrial genomes from GenBank (a systematic one-in-three sample of all 'Canis lupus familiaris' records, every wild 'Canis lupus' record, and every record of the other wild canid species), with CYTB and COX1 coding sequences extracted and compared by ungapped p-distance: at least 3 dog sequences AND at least 2 % of sampled dog sequences have their nearest non-dog sequence in a species other than Canis lupus. That outcome supports a multi-species origin.

fields.label: Fail criterion
fields.value: Zero dog sequences are nearer to a non-wolf species than to wild wolves: refutes (every maternal lineage sampled is wolf-derived). One or two such sequences (consistent with mislabelled hybrids) or the per-cent threshold unmet: mixed. If fewer than 100 dog sequences or fewer than 20 wild wolf sequences can be retrieved and parsed: inconclusive (underpowered).

fields.label: Unit
fields.value: sampled dog mitogenomes whose nearest non-dog sequence belongs to a species other than Canis lupus

fields.label: Uncertainty
fields.value: fraction 0.0000; p-distances over 2685 bp of CYTB+COX1

fields.label: Sample notes
fields.value: n dogs sampled: 446; n wild wolves: 129; alignment length bp: 2685

fields.label: Interpretation
fields.value: Darwin's 'several wild species' is read as more than one wild canid species contributing ancestry to domestic dogs. The species Darwin would have counted (wolf, jackals, coyote, dhole, African wild dog, Ethiopian wolf) are the wild canids with GenBank mitogenomes. Mitochondrial DNA tests maternal ancestry only; if even the maternal lineages are exclusively wolf-derived, the multi-species claim is refuted for the component that pre-genomic data can address, and nuclear genomic literature is cited in caveats but is not used as data. Dingoes and 'Canis lupus dingo' records are reported separately and excluded from the dog sample; records of 'Canis lupus' other than familiaris and dingo are treated as wild wolves (GenBank labels, which can include captive or admixed animals, are taken at face value). Modern taxonomy already files the dog inside Canis lupus, which the test does not assume.

fields.label: Datasets
fields.value: NCBI GenBank (nuccore) complete mitochondrial genomes of Canis lupus familiaris, wild Canis lupus, Canis latrans, Canis aureus, Canis lupaster, Canis simensis, Cuon alpinus and Lycaon pictus, retrieved through E-utilities

fields.label: Caveats
fields.value:
Every one of 446 sampled dog mitogenomes is nearer to a wild grey wolf (mean 0.15 %, maximum 0.41 % p-distance) than to any other canid species (minimum 3.0 %, to Canis lupaster); no dog maternal lineage traces to a jackal, coyote, dhole, Ethiopian wolf or African wild dog. Darwin's 'several wild species' therefore fails for maternal ancestry.

Mitochondrial DNA is a single maternally inherited locus. Nuclear-genome studies (e.g. Freedman et al. 2014 PLoS Genetics; Frantz et al. 2016 Science; Bergstrom et al. 2020 Science) reach the same conclusion, that dogs derive from one wild species, the grey wolf, possibly from more than one wolf population; those are literature, not data used here. Low-level admixture from other canids into particular dog populations would not be excluded by this test.

GenBank 'Canis lupus' records include some African wolves labelled as the former subspecies C. lupus lupaster, which is why the minimum wolf-to-other-species distance is 0.11 %; this inflates the 'wild wolf' set with a few non-wolf sequences and could only have made a non-wolf dog origin easier, not harder, to detect.

None of the dog records carries a /breed qualifier, so breed coverage of the sample cannot be documented from metadata; the 1,357 records come from many independent studies (village dogs, ancient DNA, breed panels) and the systematic one-in-three sample was fixed before any sequence was examined.

A first run dropped IUPAC ambiguity characters from the sequences, which shifted coordinates in a handful of records and produced spurious distances; the parser was corrected before the result above was produced, and the pre-registered criterion was not changed.

Taxonomic labels in GenBank are taken at face value; mislabelled wolf-dog hybrids would not affect the direction of the result.
